exampleAnswers.title: Applying Two-to-One Transformations to Random Variables

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{16}x^2, & -2 < x < 2\\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] If $Y = X^2+1,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
First, notice that the transformation $Y = X^2+1$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-2\lt x \lt 2.$

Moreover, for $-2\lt x \lt 2,$ we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $1 \le y \lt 5.$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $1 \le y < 5,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left(X^2+1 \leq y\right) \\[5pt] &= P \left(-(y-1)^{1/2} \leq X \leq (y-1)^{1/2}\right) \\[5pt] &=F_X\left((y-1)^{1/2}\right) - F_X\left(-(y-1)^{1/2}\right). \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $1 \le y < 5,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &=F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 (y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot F'_X\left((y-1)^{1/2}\right) + \dfrac12(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot F'_X\left(-(y-1)^{1/2}\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 (y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot f_X\left((y-1)^{1/2}\right) + \dfrac12(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot f_X\left(-(y-1)^{1/2}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 (y-1)^{-1/2}\left[f_X\left((y-1)^{1/2}\right)+ f_X\left(-(y-1)^{1/2}\right)\right]. \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &=\dfrac12 (y-1)^{-1/2}\left[f_X\left((y-1)^{1/2}\right) + f_X\left(-(y-1)^{1/2}\right)\right] \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 (y-1)^{-1/2}\left[\dfrac{3}{16}\left((y-1)^{1/2}\right)^2+ \dfrac{3}{16}\left(-(y-1)^{1/2}\right)^2\right] \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 (y-1)^{-1/2}\left(\dfrac{3}{16}(y-1)+ \dfrac{3}{16}(y-1)\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{16} (y-1)^{1/2}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{16} \sqrt {y-1}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{16}\sqrt {y-1}, &1 \le y < 5 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

example.title: Applying Two-to-One Transformations to Random Variables

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x}{4}, & -1 \lt x \lt 3 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] If $Y = \left(1-X\right)^2,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.explanation:
First, notice that the transformation $Y = \left(1-X\right)^2$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-1\lt x \lt 3.$

Moreover, for $-1 \lt x \lt 3,$ we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $0 \le y \lt 4.$

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 \le y < 4,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left(\left(1-X\right)^2 \leq y\right) \\[5pt] &= P \left(-y^{1/2} \leq 1-X \leq y^{1/2}\right) \\[5pt] &= P \left(-y^{1/2}-1 \leq -X \leq y^{1/2}-1\right) \\[5pt] &= P \left(1-y^{1/2} \leq X \leq 1+ y^{1/2}\right) \\[5pt] &=F_X(1+y^{1/2}) - F_X(1-y^{1/2}). \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \le y < 4,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &=F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 y^{-1/2}\cdot F'_X(1+y^{1/2}) + \dfrac12y^{-1/2}\cdot F'_X(1-y^{1/2}) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 y^{-1/2}\cdot f_X(1+y^{1/2}) + \dfrac12y^{-1/2}\cdot f_X(1-y^{1/2}) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 y^{-1/2}\left(f_X(1+y^{1/2}) + f_X(1-y^{1/2})\right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) &=\dfrac12 y^{-1/2}\left(f_X(1+y^{1/2}) + f_X(1-y^{1/2})\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac12 y^{-1/2}\left(\dfrac{1+y^{1/2}}4+ \dfrac{1-y^{1/2}}4\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac1{4} y^{-1/2}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt y}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt y}, &0 \le y < 4 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

example.title: Applying Two-to-One Transformations to Random Variables

question.text:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{12}(2-x), & -3 \lt x < 1 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

If the probability density function of $Y = X^2$ is given by \[ f_Y(y)= \begin{cases} g(y), & 0 \lt y \lt 1 \\[5pt] h(y), & 1 \leq y \lt 9 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] find the function $g(y).$
question.explanation:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y = X^2$ over the interval $-3 \lt x < 1.$

Notice the following:

  • The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $-3 \lt x \leq -1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $1 \leq y \lt 9.$

  • The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $-1 \lt x < 1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0 \lt y \lt 1.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0 \lt y \lt 1.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) & = P\big(Y \leq y\big) \\[5pt] & = P\big(X^2 \leq y \big) \\[5pt] & = P \big(-\sqrt{y} \leq X \leq \sqrt{y} \big) \\[5pt] & = F_X\big( \sqrt{y} \big) - F_X\big( -\sqrt{y} \big). \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \lt y \lt 1,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] %& = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X(\sqrt{y}) - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) \cdot F'_X(-\sqrt{y})\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X\big(\sqrt{y}\big) + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X\big(-\sqrt{y}\big)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot f_X\big(\sqrt{y}\big) + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot f_X\big(-\sqrt{y}\big)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left( f_X\big(\sqrt{y}\big) + f_X\big(-\sqrt{y}\big) \right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left( f_X\big(\sqrt{y}\big) + f_X\big(-\sqrt{y}\big) \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left( \dfrac{1}{12}\big(2 - \sqrt{y}\big) + \dfrac{1}{12}\big(2 + \sqrt{y}\big) \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{6\sqrt{y}}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $g(y) = \dfrac{1}{6\sqrt{y}}.$

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{5}, & 0 < x < 5 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] If the probability density function of $Y = (X-3)^2$ is given by \[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} g(y), & 0 \lt y \lt 4 \\[5pt] h(y), & 4 \leq y \lt 9 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] find the function $g(y).$
question.explanation:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y = (X-3)^2$ over the interval $0 < x < 5.$

Notice the following:

  • The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $0 \lt x \leq 1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $4 \leq y \lt 9.$

  • The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $1 < x < 5.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0 \lt y \lt 4.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0 \lt y \lt 4.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 \lt y \lt 4,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] &= P\left((X-3)^2 \leq y \right) \\[5pt] & = P\left(-\sqrt{y} \leq X - 3 \leq \sqrt{y} \right) \\[5pt] & = P\left(3 - \sqrt{y} \leq X \leq 3 + \sqrt{y} \right) \\[5pt] & = F_X\left( 3 + \sqrt{y} \right) - F_X\left( 3 - \sqrt{y} \right). \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \lt y \lt 4,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] %& = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X\left( 3 + \sqrt{y} \right) - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \right) \cdot F'_X\left( 3 - \sqrt{y} \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X\left( 3 + \sqrt{y} \right) + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X\left( 3 - \sqrt{y} \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot f_X\left( 3 + \sqrt{y} \right) + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot f_X\left( 3 - \sqrt{y} \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left(f_X\left( 3 + \sqrt{y} \right) + f_X\left( 3 - \sqrt{y} \right) \right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left( f_X\left( 3 + \sqrt{y} \right) + f_X\left( 3 - \sqrt{y} \right) \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left( \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{5} \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt{y}}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $g(y) = \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt{y}}.$

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{8}x, & 0 < x < 4 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] If the probability density function of $Y = \dfrac{1}{2}|X - 1|$ is given by \[ f_Y(y)= \begin{cases} g(y), & 0 \lt y \lt \dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] h(y), & \dfrac{1}{2} \leq y \lt \dfrac{3}{2} \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] find the function $h(y).$
question.explanation:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y = \dfrac{1}{2}|X - 1|$ over the interval $0 < x < 4.$

Notice the following:

  • The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $0 < x \lt 2.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0 \lt y \lt \dfrac{1}{2}.$

  • The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $2 \leq x \lt 4.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $\dfrac{1}{2} \leq y \lt \dfrac{3}{2}.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $\dfrac{1}{2} \leq y \lt \dfrac{3}{2}.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $\dfrac{1}{2} \leq y \lt \dfrac{3}{2},$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) & = P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] & = P\left(\dfrac{1}{2}|X-1| \leq y \right) \\[5pt] & = P\left(|X-1| \leq 2y \right) \\[5pt] & = P\left(X - 1 \leq 2y \right) \\[5pt] & = P \left(X \leq 2y + 1 \right) \\[5pt] & = F_X( 2y+1 ). \end{align*} Notice that we used $|X-1| = X-1$ for $X > 1.$

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $\dfrac{1}{2} \leq y \lt \dfrac{3}{2},$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] & = 2 F'_X( 2y+1 )\\[5pt] & = 2 f_X( 2y+1 ). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = 2 f_X( 2y+1 )\\[5pt] & = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{8}(2y+1)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{4}(2y+1). \end{align*}

Consequently, $h(y) = \dfrac{1}{4}(2y+1).$

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} e^{2-x}, & x \geq 2\\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] If the probability density function of $Y = (X-4)^2$ is given by \[ f_Y(y)= \begin{cases} g(y), & 0 \lt y \lt 4 \\[5pt] h(y), & y \geq 4 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] find the function $g(y).$
question.explanation:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y = (X-4)^2$ over the interval $x \geq 2.$

Notice the following:

  • The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $2 \lt x \lt 6.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0 \lt y \lt 4.$

  • The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $x \geq 6.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $y \geq 4.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0 \lt y \lt 4.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 \lt y \lt 4,$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) & = P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] & = P\left((X-4)^{2} \leq y\right) \\[5pt] & = P \left( - \sqrt{y} \leq X-4 \leq \sqrt{y} \right) \\[5pt] & = P \left(4 - \sqrt{y} \leq X \leq 4 + \sqrt{y} \right) \\[5pt] & = F_X( 4 + \sqrt{y} ) - F_X( 4 - \sqrt{y} ). \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \lt y \lt 4,$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] %& = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X( 4 + \sqrt{y} ) - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) \cdot F'_X(4 - \sqrt{y})\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X( 4 + \sqrt{y} ) + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot F'_X(4 - \sqrt{y})\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot f_X( 4 + \sqrt{y} ) + \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \cdot f_X(4 - \sqrt{y})\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left( f_X( 4 + \sqrt{y} ) + f_X(4 - \sqrt{y}) \right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left( f_X( 4 + \sqrt{y} ) + f_X(4 - \sqrt{y}) \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \left(e^{2 - 4 - \sqrt{y}} + e^{2 - 4 + \sqrt{y}} \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{-\sqrt{y} - 2} + e^{\sqrt{y} - 2}}{2\sqrt{y}}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $g(y) = \dfrac{e^{-\sqrt{y} - 2} + e^{\sqrt{y} - 2}}{2\sqrt{y}}.$

question.text: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: \[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{8}x, & 0 < x < 4 \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases}\] If the probability density function of $Y = \dfrac{1}{2}|X - 1|$ is given by \[ f_Y(y)= \begin{cases} g(y), & 0 \lt y \lt \dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] h(y), & \dfrac{1}{2} \leq y \lt \dfrac{3}{2} \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \] find the function $g(y).$
question.explanation:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y = \dfrac{1}{2}|X - 1|$ over the interval $0 < x < 4.$

Notice the following:

  • The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $0 < x \lt 2.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0 \lt y \lt \dfrac{1}{2}.$

  • The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $2 \leq x \lt 4.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $\dfrac{1}{2} \leq y \lt \dfrac{3}{2}.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0 \lt y \lt \dfrac{1}{2}.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0 \lt y \lt \dfrac{1}{2},$ we have \begin{align*} F_Y(y) & = P(Y \leq y) \\[5pt] & = P\left(\dfrac{1}{2}|X-1| \leq y \right) \\[5pt] & = P\left(|X-1| \leq 2y \right) \\[5pt] & = P \left( - 2y \leq X-1 \leq 2y \right) \\[5pt] & = P \left(1 - 2y \leq X \leq 2y + 1 \right) \\[5pt] & = F_X( 2y+1 ) - F_X( 1-2y ). \end{align*}

To compute the PDF $f_Y(y)$ for $0 \lt y \lt \dfrac{1}{2},$ we differentiate $F_Y$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = F'_Y(y) \\[5pt] %& = 2 \cdot F'_X( 2y+1 ) - (-2) \cdot F'_X( 1-2y )\\[5pt] & = 2 F'_X( 2y+1 ) + 2 F'_X( 1-2y )\\[5pt] & = 2 f_X( 2y+1 ) + 2 f_X( 1-2y )\\[5pt] & = 2 \left( f_X( 2y+1 ) + f_X( 1-2y ) \right). \end{align*}

Applying the definition of $f_X,$ we finally arrive at \begin{align*} f_Y(y) & = 2 \left( f_X( 2y+1 ) + f_X( 1-2y ) \right)\\[5pt] & = 2 \left( \dfrac{1}{8}(2y+1) + \dfrac{1}{8}(1-2y) \right)\\[5pt] & = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align*}

Consequently, $g(y) = \dfrac{1}{2}.$
